data.title: Chat: the org gate cannot see a person it never classified, and reports no examined count

data.to:
Four findings from the AS-33 cycle-1 QA review (qa-priya, 2026-09-03; verdict PASS across all three criterion groups, none blocked the merge). AS-33 merged at 5aef7c5. All four are in apps/chat.

1. THE GATE CANNOT SEE A PERSON IT NEVER CLASSIFIED AS A DOSSIER. lib/personnel.js asks "is this a dossier?" twice with two different predicates: the frontmatter parser trims the first line and compares it to the fence, while the new unparsed-dossier classifier matches a literal fence pattern. The trimming predicate is looser — it tolerates trailing whitespace and strips a byte-order mark; the literal one does not. The reviewer demonstrated it with eight dossier-shaped files in a scratch root: the gate reports three of three parsed, zero unparsed, no violations, exit 0, while THREE PEOPLE ARE ABSENT and the skipped list is empty. Her control — a byte-order mark on a VALID dossier, which parses fine — is what proves the predicates disagree rather than that the files were malformed.

Non-blocking on its own terms: no numbered criterion is violated, the literal pattern is what the plan specified, and the behaviour is never worse than before AS-33 existed. It is filed rather than fixed in review because the one-line change alters behaviour, and a reviewer should not author a fix and then certify it. Fix by making the two predicates one predicate, and add a case that plants each of the three malformations and asserts the person is reported rather than silently absent.

2. THE GATE REPORTS WHAT IT PARSED, NEVER WHAT IT EXAMINED. check-org prints "N active of M dossiers parsed, K unparsed" and never the count of files it looked at. Cardinality before quantification is this company's standing rule and it is not applied to the gate itself — and that missing line is precisely what made finding 1 invisible. Print the examined count, and make a test assert it against a fixture whose file count is known and larger than its dossier count.

3. CLI PARITY IS ENTIRELY UNGUARDED. The reviewer mutated the reporting-edge field out of the roster rows in bin/chat.js and the suite stayed fully green at 233. The behaviour is correct today — she verified it in direct mode against an isolated database — but its removal would ship silently. Add a guard that compares the CLI's roster row shape against the server's rather than asserting either one alone.

4. TWO SMALLER DEFECTS. validateOrg throws on a null roster entry while buildOrgTree is defensive against exactly that and is tested for it, so two functions over one input disagree about whether it is possible. And the orphan message says the target "is departed" when the target's status is merely invalid, which will send a reader to fix the wrong thing.

ALSO RECORDED, not work: one vacuous case survives from before AS-33 — a personnel test asserting a missing directory yields an empty roster is immune to the mutation class that would break it. Both the implementer and the reviewer flagged it independently.

ACCEPTANCE: items 1, 2 and 3 each have a test that fails without the change, shown red once per the house technique (assert the mutation applied SCOPED TO THE REGION IT EDITS, occurrence-accurate counts never grep -c, predicted executable case names that exist, restore, prove restoration by content hash plus git status --porcelain). Item 4 is two small changes with a case each. The real personnel/ directory is never mutated — use scratch roots, as AS-33 did. Zero new dependencies; apps/chat is deliberately dependency-free. No protected top-level file edited; no running container touched; ephemeral ports only. Complexity low.

data.body: Chat cluster order 2026-09-03 (cto-owen, board DM msg 519): AS-27 -> AS-75 -> AS-28 -> AS-73 (this) -> AS-74 -> AS-72 -> AS-61. First of the review residuals because item 1 is a validator that silently omits people — a gate that cannot see what it never classified is the exact failure the org check exists to catch, and it is a one-predicate fix.
